text: The CMA must prepare and publish a statement of policy in relation to the exercise of powers to impose a monetary penalty under this Chapter. The statement must include a statement about the considerations relevant to the determination of— whether to impose a penalty under this Chapter, and the nature and amount of any such penalty. The CMA may revise its statement of policy and, where it does so, must publish the revised statement. In preparing or revising its statement of policy the CMA must consult— the Secretary of State, and such other persons as the CMA considers appropriate. A statement of policy, or revised statement, may not be published under this section without the approval of the Secretary of State. Subsection (7) applies where the CMA proposes to impose under this Chapter a monetary penalty on a person. The CMA must have regard to the statement of policy most recently published under this section at the time of the act or omission giving rise to the penalty in deciding— whether to impose the penalty, and if so, the nature and amount of the penalty.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.199

metadata.act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
heading_breadcrumb: Statement of policy in relation to monetary penalties
commentary: S. 199 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: This section applies where— the CMA gives to a body corporate (“the respondent”) a final notice, and the interconnection condition applies in relation to the respondent. The interconnection condition applies in relation to the respondent if— at the time the final notice is given, the respondent is a member of a group of interconnected bodies corporate, at any time when requirements imposed by the final notice remain in force, the respondent becomes a member of a group of interconnected bodies corporate, or at any time when requirements imposed by the final notice remain in force, a group of interconnected bodies corporate of which the respondent is a member is increased by the addition of one or more further members. The notice may include provision for the requirements (or any particular requirements) imposed by the final notice on the respondent also to be binding upon all other members of the group (in addition to the respondent), as if each of them were the respondent. Provision may be included in a notice under subsection (3) only if the CMA considers it just, reasonable and proportionate to include that provision. A group of interconnected bodies corporate is a group consisting of two or more bodies corporate all of whom are interconnected with each other. Any two bodies corporate are interconnected— if one of them is a subsidiary of the other, or if both of them are subsidiaries of the same body corporate. Where a final notice includes provision under subsection (3), the notice must also be given to any other member of the respondent’s group in relation to which the requirements imposed by the notice are to be binding. In this section “final notice” means— a final infringement notice, an online interface notice, or a final breach of directions enforcement notice.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.200

metadata.act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
commentary: S. 200 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: The CMA must keep a record of— undertakings it has accepted and enforcement directions it has given, and reviews it has carried out in relation to the effectiveness of such undertakings and directions. If requested to do so by the Secretary of State, the CMA must prepare a report on— the effectiveness of undertakings and enforcement directions, and the number and outcome of appeals brought under section 202. The CMA must— provide to the Secretary of State a report prepared under this section, and publish the report in such manner as the CMA considers appropriate. In this section— “undertakings” means undertakings given under section 185; “enforcement directions” includes directions given in a notice under section 192(5)(b).
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.201

metadata.act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
commentary: S. 201 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: A person to whom a relevant notice is given may appeal to the appropriate appeal court against— a decision to impose a monetary penalty by virtue of the notice, the nature or amount of any such penalty, or the giving of directions by virtue of the notice. The grounds for an appeal under subsection (1)(a) or (b) are that— the decision to impose a monetary penalty was based on an error of fact, the decision was wrong in law, the amount of the penalty is unreasonable, or the decision was unreasonable or wrong for any other reason. The grounds for an appeal under subsection (1)(c) are that— the decision to give the directions was based on an error of fact, the decision was wrong in law, the nature of the directions is unreasonable, or the decision was unreasonable or wrong for any other reason. On an appeal under this section the appropriate appeal court may quash, confirm or vary the relevant notice. Except in the case of an appeal relating to a final false information enforcement notice, in addition to the powers conferred by subsection (4) the appropriate appeal court may also remit any matter that is the subject of the appeal to the CMA. An appeal under this section must be brought before the end of the applicable period beginning with the day on which the relevant notice was given to the person seeking to bring the appeal. The appropriate appeal court may extend the applicable period for bringing an appeal. Where an appeal is brought in respect of— a requirement to pay a monetary penalty, or a requirement to pay compensation under directions imposing enhanced consumer measures, the penalty or compensation is not required to be paid until after the appeal is determined, withdrawn or otherwise dealt with. In this section— “applicable period” means— in relation to a final false information enforcement notice, the period of 28 days; in relation to any other relevant notice, the period of 60 days; “appropriate appeal court” means— in relation to England and Wales or Northern Ireland, the High Court; in relation to Scotland, the Outer House of the Court of Session; “relevant notice” means— a final infringement notice, an online interface notice, a final breach of undertakings enforcement notice, a final breach of directions enforcement notice, or a final false information enforcement notice.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.202

metadata.act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
commentary: S. 202 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: An order or notice under Chapter 3 or 4 under which a person (“the respondent”) is required to pay a monetary penalty must state the following information (referred to in those Chapters as the “monetary penalty information”)— the amount of the penalty (including whether it is a fixed amount, an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate or both a fixed amount and an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate); the grounds on which the penalty is imposed together with any other factors that the court (in the case of an order) or the CMA (in the case of a notice) considers justify the giving of the penalty or its amount; in the case of an amount calculated by reference to a daily rate, the day on which the amount first starts to accumulate and the day or days on which it might cease to accumulate; how the penalty is to be paid; the date or dates, no earlier than the end of the applicable period beginning with the date on which the order was served on or the notice was given to the respondent, by which the penalty or (as the case may be) different portions of it are required to be paid; that the penalty or (as the case may be) different portions of it may be paid earlier than the date or dates by which it or they are required to be paid; that the respondent has the right to apply under subsection (3) (in the case of an order) or subsection (4) (in the case of a notice); the rights available to the respondent to appeal in respect of the imposition of the penalty; the main details of the rights mentioned in paragraphs (g) and (h). In subsection (1)(e) “the applicable period” means— in the case of an order or a final false information enforcement notice, the period of 28 days; in any other case, the period of 60 days. The respondent may, within 14 days of the date on which an order imposing a monetary penalty is served on the respondent, apply to the court for the court to specify a different date or dates by which the penalty, or different portions of it, are to be paid. The respondent may, within 14 days of the date on which a notice imposing a monetary penalty is given to the respondent, apply to the CMA to specify a different date or dates by which the penalty, or different portions of it, are required to be paid. References in subsections (1) and (2) to an order include references to a notice accompanying such an order given under section 158(4). In the application of this section to Scotland, the references in subsections (1)(e) and (3) to an order being served include service of an extract order in execution of or diligence on the order.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.203

metadata.act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
heading_breadcrumb: Information to accompany orders or notices imposing monetary penalties

text: In this Part references to “turnover” of a person include— turnover both in and outside the United Kingdom; where the person controls another person, the turnover of that other person; where the person is controlled by another person, the turnover of that person. text: This section applies where a monetary penalty imposed under Chapter 4, or any part of such a penalty, has not been paid by the date on which it is required to be paid and— an appeal to a court against the imposition of the penalty has not been brought before the end of the period within which it is required to be brought, or any such appeal that was brought has been determined, withdrawn or otherwise disposed of. The CMA may recover from the person on whom the penalty was imposed any of the penalty and any interest which has not been paid. Any such penalty and interest may be recovered summarily (or, in Scotland, recovered) as a civil debt by the CMA. Subsection (5) applies where— a penalty is payable by a person by virtue of a final infringement notice, the notice also includes directions imposing a requirement on the person to take enhanced consumer measures, and the enhanced consumer measures that the person is required to take are or include redress measures (see section 221(2)). In deciding whether to recover the penalty from the person under subsection (2), the CMA must have regard to— whether any compensation required to be paid to consumers under the redress measures has been, or is likely to be, paid, and where any such payments have not yet been paid (in full or in part), the effect that recovery of the penalty from the person may have on the person’s ability to make those compensatory payments.

text: If the whole or any portion of a monetary penalty imposed is not paid by the date by which it is required to be paid, the unpaid balance from time to time carries interest at the statutory rate. Where an application has been made under section 203(3) or (4), the penalty is not required to be paid until the application has been determined, withdrawn or otherwise disposed of. Where an application has been made to appeal to a court in respect of a monetary penalty, the penalty is not required to be paid until the application has been determined, withdrawn or otherwise disposed of. If a portion of a monetary penalty imposed by an order of the court has not been paid by the date required for it, the court may, where it considers it appropriate to do so, by order require so much of the penalty as has not already been paid (and is capable of being paid immediately) to be paid immediately. If a portion of a monetary penalty imposed by virtue of a notice given by the CMA has not been paid by the date required for it, the CMA may, where it considers it appropriate to do so, by notice require so much of the penalty as has not already been paid (and is capable of being paid immediately) to be paid immediately. Where on an appeal under section 202 the court substitutes a penalty of a different nature or of a lesser amount, the court may require the payment of interest at the statutory rate on the substituted penalty from whatever date it considers appropriate (which may include a date before the determination of the appeal). In the case of a monetary penalty imposed on a firm that is not a body corporate, the penalty is to be paid out of the assets or funds of the firm. Sums received from a person towards payment of a monetary penalty must be paid— in the case of a penalty imposed by an order of the Court of Session or the Sheriff, into the Scottish Consolidated Fund; in the case of a penalty imposed by an order of a court in Northern Ireland, into the Consolidated Fund of Northern Ireland; in any other case, into the Consolidated Fund of the United Kingdom. In this section— “monetary penalty” means a monetary penalty imposed under Chapter 3 or 4; “the statutory rate” means the rate for the time being specified in section 17 of the Judgments Act 1838.

text: This section provides for how references to the supply of goods or digital content are to be read for the purposes of this Part. References to a person who supplies goods or digital content are to be read as including references to a person who seeks to supply goods or digital content (and references to a person who receives goods or digital content are to be read in a corresponding way). text: This section applies for the purposes of this Part. A person has a special relationship with a body corporate if the person is— a controller of the body corporate, or a director, manager, secretary or other similar officer of the body corporate or a person purporting to act in such a capacity. A person is a controller of a body corporate if— the directors of the body corporate, or of another body corporate which is its controller, are accustomed to act in accordance with the person’s directions or instructions, or either alone or with one or more associates, the person is entitled to exercise or control the exercise of one third or more of the voting power at any general meeting of the body corporate or of another body corporate which is its controller. A person (“P”) is an associate of an individual if— P is the spouse or civil partner of the individual; P is a relative of the individual; P is a relative of the individual’s spouse or civil partner; P is the spouse or civil partner of a relative of the individual; P is a spouse or civil partner of a relative of the individual’s spouse or civil partner; P lives in the same household as the individual otherwise than merely because P, or the individual, is the other’s employer, tenant, lodger or boarder; P is the relative of a person who is an associate of the individual by virtue of paragraph (f); P has at some time in the past fallen within any of paragraphs (a) to (g); P is in partnership with the individual; the individual is an associate of an individual with whom P is in partnership. A person (“P”) is an associate of a body corporate if— P is a controller of the body corporate, or P is an associate of a person who is a controller of the body corporate. A body corporate is an associate of another body corporate if— the same person is a controller of both; a person (“P”) is a controller of one and persons who are P’s associates are controllers of the other; a person (“P”) is a controller of one and P and persons who are P’s associates are controllers of the other; a group of two or more persons is a controller of each company and the groups consist of the same persons; a group of two or more persons is a controller of each company and the groups may be regarded as consisting of the same persons by treating (in one or more cases) a member of either group as replaced by a person of whom that person is an associate. In this section “relative” means a brother, sister, uncle, aunt, nephew, niece, lineal ancestor or lineal descendant.

text: References in this Part to “enhanced consumer measures” are references to— redress measures (see subsection (2)), compliance measures (see subsection (3)), or choice measures (see subsection (4)). Redress measures are— measures offering compensation or other redress to affected consumers; in cases where the commercial practice constituting a relevant infringement relates to a contract, measures enabling affected consumers the option to terminate (but not vary) the contract; in cases where the affected consumers cannot be identified, or cannot be identified without disproportionate cost to the person giving the undertaking in question or against whom the order in question is made, measures intended to be in the collective interests of consumers. Compliance measures are measures intended to prevent, or reduce the risk of the occurrence or repetition of, the infringing conduct (which may include measures imposed for the purpose of improving compliance with consumer law more generally). Choice measures are measures intended to enable consumers to choose more effectively between persons supplying goods, services or digital content. In this section— references to affected consumers are references to consumers who have suffered loss as a result of the infringing conduct or who have otherwise been affected in any other way by the conduct; references to the “infringing conduct” are to the conduct that has given rise to the enforcement order or undertaking concerned.

text: This Chapter confers protections on consumers from unfair commercial practices. Section 225 sets out what are unfair commercial practices and prohibits the use and promotion of them. Sections 226 to 230 provide more detail about commercial practices which are unfair because they are misleading, aggressive or omit material information, or because they contravene the requirements of professional diligence. Section 231 requires, or confers power on, specified public bodies to enforce the prohibitions in section 225. Sections 232 to 235 confer rights on consumers in relation to unfair commercial practices and make related provision. Section 236 sets out what happens when a trader supplies a product to a consumer that the consumer has not requested. Sections 237 to 241 create criminal offences in relation to unfair commercial practices and make related provision. Sections 242 to 252 contain miscellaneous and interpretative provisions in relation to this Chapter.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.224

text: Unfair commercial practices are prohibited. The promotion of unfair commercial practices in, or in connection with, a code of conduct by— a person responsible for the content of a code of conduct, or a person responsible for monitoring compliance with a code of conduct, is prohibited. In this Chapter— “commercial practice” means an act or omission by a trader relating to the promotion or supply of— the trader’s product to a consumer, another trader’s product to a consumer, or a consumer’s product to the trader or another person; “consumer” means an individual acting for purposes that are wholly or mainly outside the individual’s business; “trader” means— a person (“P”) acting for purposes relating to P’s business, or a person acting in the name of, or on behalf of, P for purposes relating to P’s business. A commercial practice is unfair if— it is likely to cause the average consumer to take a transactional decision that the consumer would not have taken otherwise as a result of the practice involving one or more of the following— a misleading action (see section 226); a misleading omission (see section 227); an aggressive practice (see section 228); a contravention of the requirements of professional diligence (see section 229), it omits material information from an invitation to purchase (see section 230), or it is listed in Schedule 20 (commercial practices which are in all circumstances considered unfair). It is immaterial for the purposes of the definition of “commercial practice” in subsection (3) whether the act or omission takes place— at the time of the promotion or supply in question, or before or after that time. It is immaterial for the purposes of the definition of “trader” in subsection (3)— in relation to paragraph (a) of that definition, whether P is acting personally or through another person acting in P’s name or on P’s behalf; in relation to paragraph (b) of that definition, whether or not the purposes relating to P’s business are the only or main purposes for which the person is acting.

text: For the purposes of this Chapter, a commercial practice involves a misleading action if the practice involves— the provision of false or misleading information relating to a product, a trader or any other matter relevant to a transactional decision, an overall presentation which is likely to deceive the average consumer about a matter relating to a product, a trader or any other matter relevant to a transactional decision, any marketing of a product which creates confusion, or is likely to create confusion, with any product, trade mark, trade name or other distinguishing mark of another trader, or a failure to comply with a requirement in a code of conduct to which subsection (5) applies in circumstances where the trader asserts that the trader acts in compliance with that code. In subsection (1)(a), the reference to misleading information includes a reference to information which, although true, is presented in a misleading way. For the purposes of subsection (1)(b), an overall presentation may be deceiving even if the information it contains is true. In subsection (1)(c), the reference to another trader is a reference to a trader other than the trader supplying the product that is being marketed. This subsection applies to a requirement in a code of conduct if— there is no discretion afforded to the trader in relation to the requirement, and compliance with the requirement is capable of being verified.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.226

metadata.act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024

text: For the purposes of this Chapter, a commercial practice involves a misleading omission if, considering the matters mentioned in subsection (3), the practice— omits material information, omits information which the trader is required under any other enactment to give to a consumer as part of the practice, or fails to identify its commercial intent (unless it is already apparent from the context). In subsection (1)(a), “material information” means information that the average consumer needs to take an informed transactional decision. The matters referred to in subsection (1) are— any limitations resulting from the means of communication used in the commercial practice (including limitations of space or time), and any steps taken by the trader to overcome those limitations by providing information by other means. In this section, references to omitting information include providing information— in a way that is unclear or untimely, or in such a way that the consumer is unlikely to see it.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.227

text: For the purposes of this Chapter, a commercial practice involves an aggressive practice if it uses harassment, coercion or undue influence. In determining whether a commercial practice uses harassment, coercion or undue influence, account must be taken of— the nature of the practice; the timing and location of the practice; whether the practice involves the use of any threatening or abusive language or behaviour; whether the practice exploits any vulnerability of a consumer (including any vulnerability of a kind mentioned in section 247(4)); whether the practice involves a threat to take action which cannot legally be taken; whether the practice requires a consumer to take onerous or disproportionate action in order to exercise rights that the consumer has in relation to a product. In this section— “coercion” includes the use or threat of physical force; “undue influence” means exploiting a position of power in relation to a consumer so as to apply pressure in a way which significantly limits the consumer’s ability to make an informed decision.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.228

text: For the purposes of this Chapter, a commercial practice involves a contravention of the requirements of professional diligence if the practice falls short of the standard of skill and care which a trader may reasonably be expected to exercise towards consumers which is commensurate with either— honest market practice in the trader’s field of activity, or the general principle of good faith in the trader’s field of activity.

text: For the purposes of this Chapter, a commercial practice which is an invitation to purchase omits material information if, considering the matters mentioned in subsection (8), it omits any of the information which is— set out in subsection (2), and not already apparent from the context. The information referred to in subsection (1) is— the main characteristics of the product (to the extent appropriate considering the means used to communicate the invitation to purchase and the nature of the product); the total price of the product (so far as paragraph (c) does not apply); if, owing to the nature of the product, the whole or any part of the total price cannot reasonably be calculated in advance, how the price (or that part of it) will be calculated; the identity of the trader and the identity of any other person on whose behalf the trader is acting; the business address and, if different, the service address of the trader and any business email address of the trader; in relation to any other person on whose behalf the trader is acting— the person’s business address and business email address (if the person has such addresses), and if different to the person’s business address, the person’s service address; any freight, delivery or postal charges, including any taxes, not included in the total price of the product but which the consumer may choose to incur (or where those additional charges or taxes cannot reasonably be calculated in advance, the fact that they may be payable); for products involving a right of withdrawal or cancellation, the existence of such a right; to the extent that the trader’s practice in relation to any of the arrangements mentioned in subsection (3) departs from the trader’s published practice in relation to those arrangements, the practice which the trader is currently operating; any information which the trader is required under any other enactment to give to a consumer as part of an invitation to purchase. The arrangements referred to in subsection (2)(i) are— the arrangements for payment; the arrangements for delivery of the product; the arrangements for performance; the arrangements for handling complaints. For the purposes of subsection (2)(b) the total price of a product includes any fees, taxes, charges or other payments that the consumer will necessarily incur if the consumer purchases the product. For the purposes of subsection (2)(c) (and subject to the matters mentioned in subsection (8)) the information given must— be such that it enables the consumer to calculate the total price, and be set out with as much prominence as any information that is set out in compliance with subsection (2)(b). For the purposes of subsection (2)(d) “identity”, in relation to a trader, means— the name of the trader, and if different, the name under which the trader trades. For the purposes of subsection (2)(e)— “business address”, in relation to a person, means— where the person is a body corporate, the address of its registered or principal office, where the person is a firm that is not a body corporate, the address of the principal office of the firm, or in a case where neither paragraph (a) or (b) applies, the address of the person’s principal place of business; “business email address”, in relation to a person, means any email address used by the person for conducting business; “service address”, in relation to a person, means the address at which the person will accept service of documents. The matters referred to in subsection (1) are— any limitations resulting from the means of communication used in the commercial practice (including limitations of space or time), and any steps taken by the trader to overcome those limitations by providing information by other means. In this section, references to omitting information include providing information— in a way that is unclear or untimely, or in such a way that the consumer is unlikely to see it. In this Chapter, “invitation to purchase” means a commercial practice involving the provision of information to a consumer— which indicates the characteristics of a product and its price, and which enables, or purports to enable, the consumer to decide whether to purchase the product or take another transactional decision in relation to the product.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.230

text: It is the duty of every local weights and measures authority in Great Britain to enforce in its area the prohibitions in section 225. It is the duty of the Department for the Economy in Northern Ireland to enforce the prohibitions in section 225 in Northern Ireland. The CMA may also enforce the provisions of this Chapter. In exercising functions under this section, every local weights and measures authority in Great Britain, the Department for the Economy in Northern Ireland and the CMA must have regard to the desirability of encouraging control of unfair commercial practices by such established means as it considers appropriate having regard to all the circumstances of the particular case. Nothing in this section authorises a local weights and measures authority in Great Britain to bring proceedings in Scotland for an offence.

text: A consumer has rights of redress under this Chapter if each of the following four conditions is met. The first condition is that— the consumer enters into a contract with a trader under which the trader supplies a product to the consumer (a “business-to-consumer contract”), the consumer enters into a contract with a trader under which— the consumer supplies a product to the trader, and the trader does not supply a product to the consumer (a “consumer-to-business contract”), or the consumer makes a payment to the trader for the supply of a product (a “consumer payment”). The second condition is that— the trader engages in a prohibited practice in relation to the product, or in a case where a consumer enters into a business-to-consumer contract for goods or digital content— a producer engages in a prohibited practice in relation to the goods or digital content, and when the contract is entered into, the trader is aware of the commercial practice that constitutes the prohibited practice or could reasonably be expected to be aware of it. The third condition is that the prohibited practice is a significant factor in the consumer’s decision— to enter into the contract mentioned in subsection (2)(a) or (b), or to make the payment mentioned in subsection (2)(c). The fourth condition is that the product concerned is not a product excluded from the application of rights of redress by regulations under section 233. In subsection (3), “producer” means— a manufacturer of the goods or digital content, an importer of the goods or digital content into the United Kingdom, or a person purporting to be such a manufacturer or importer by placing the person’s name, trade mark or other distinctive sign on the goods or by using it in connection with the digital content, and includes a producer acting personally or through another person acting in the producer’s name or on the producer’s behalf. In this Chapter, “prohibited practice” means an unfair commercial practice involving— a misleading action, or an aggressive practice. For the purposes of subsection (7), section 225(4)(a) applies as if the reference to a transactional decision were a reference to any decision taken by a consumer to— enter into a business-to-consumer contract, enter into a consumer-to-business contract, or make a consumer payment.

text: The Secretary of State may by regulations provide for any of the following descriptions of rights to be exercisable by a consumer who has rights of redress under this Chapter— a right to unwind in respect of a relevant contract or consumer payment; a right to a discount in respect of a supply of a product under a relevant contract; a right to damages in respect of financial loss, distress or physical inconvenience or discomfort. Regulations under this section may include provision— about how a right is to be exercised by the consumer; for an amount of discount mentioned in subsection (1)(b) to be determined in accordance with the regulations; about the circumstances in which damages mentioned in subsection (1)(c) are or are not payable; imposing conditions or restrictions on the exercise of a right; about the consequences of the exercise of a right; excluding products of a description specified in the regulations from the application of the rights of redress available under this Chapter. Provision under subsection (2)(e) about the consequences of the exercise of a right may (among other things)— provide for the termination of a relevant contract; require the trader to make a refund of an amount determined in accordance with the regulations; require goods supplied under a relevant contract to be returned or for payment to be made in respect of such goods. In this section, “relevant contract” means— a business-to-consumer contract; a consumer-to-business contract. Regulations under this section are subject to the affirmative procedure.

text: A consumer with a right to unwind, a right to a discount or a right to damages by virtue of regulations under section 233 may bring a claim in civil proceedings to enforce that right. In Scotland, proceedings to enforce a right to unwind may be brought before the Sheriff or the Court of Session. If in proceedings under this section the consumer establishes that the consumer has one of the rights mentioned in subsection (1), the court must make an order that gives effect to— that right, and any associated obligations of the consumer imposed by regulations under section 233. The Limitation Act 1980 applies to a claim under this section in England and Wales as if it were an action founded on simple contract. The Limitation (Northern Ireland) Order 1989 (S.I. 1989/1339 (N.I. 11)) applies to a claim under this section in Northern Ireland as if it were an action founded on simple contract.

text: Nothing in this Chapter affects the ability of a consumer to make a claim under a rule of law or equity, or under an enactment, in respect of conduct constituting a prohibited practice. text: This section applies where a trader engages in the unfair commercial practice described at paragraph 31 of Schedule 20. The consumer is exempted from any obligation to pay for (or provide any other consideration for) the products supplied by the trader. In the case of a supply of goods that has not been requested, the consumer may, as between the consumer and the trader, use, deal with or dispose of the goods as if they were an unconditional gift to the consumer. The absence of a response from a consumer following the supply of the product does not constitute consent from the consumer to comply with the trader’s demand for the consumer to— pay for the product; return the product; safely store the product.

text: A trader commits an offence if, in breach of section 225(1), the trader engages in an unfair commercial practice which involves a misleading action within section 226(1)(a), (b) or (c) (see section 225(4)(a)(i)). A trader commits an offence if, in breach of section 225(1), the trader engages in an unfair commercial practice which involves a misleading omission (see section 225(4)(a)(ii)). A trader commits an offence if, in breach of section 225(1), the trader engages in an unfair commercial practice which involves an aggressive practice (see section 225(4)(a)(iii)). A trader commits an offence if, in breach of section 225(1)— the trader engages in an unfair commercial practice which involves a contravention of the requirements of professional diligence (see section 225(4)(a)(iv)), and the trader knows, or is reckless as to whether, the commercial practice involves a contravention of the requirements of professional diligence. For the purposes of subsection (4) a trader who fails to have regard to whether a commercial practice involves a contravention of the requirements of professional diligence is to be treated as being reckless as to whether it does (regardless of whether the trader has reason to believe that it might). A trader commits an offence if, in breach of section 225(1), the trader engages in an unfair commercial practice by omitting material information from an invitation to purchase (see section 225(4)(b)). A trader commits an offence if, in breach of section 225(1), the trader engages in a commercial practice which is unfair by virtue of it being of a description listed in Schedule 20 (see section 225(4)(c)) other than an excluded description. The following are excluded descriptions for the purposes of subsection (7)— the description of practice mentioned in paragraph 12 of Schedule 20; the descriptions of practices mentioned in paragraph 13 of that Schedule; the description of practice mentioned in paragraph 30 of that Schedule.

text: It is a defence for a person (“the defendant”) charged with an offence under subsection (1), (2), (3), (6) or (7) of section 237 to prove— that the commission of the offence was due to— the act or omission of another person, reliance on information given by another person, a mistake or accident, or another cause beyond the defendant’s control, and that the defendant took all reasonable precautions and exercised all due diligence to avoid the commission of such an offence by the defendant or any other person under the defendant’s control. Subsection (3) applies in a case where a person (“the defendant”) has been charged with an offence under subsection (1), (2), (3), (6) or (7) of section 237 alleged to have been committed by the publication of an advertisement. It is a defence for the defendant to prove that— the defendant’s business is to publish or arrange for the publication of advertisements, the defendant received the advertisement for publication in the ordinary course of business, and the defendant did not know and had no reason to suspect that its publication would amount to the offence with which the defendant is charged. A defendant is not entitled to rely on the defence provided by subsection (1) by reason of the matters referred to in paragraph (a)(i) or (a)(ii) of that subsection without the permission of the court unless— the defendant has served on the prosecutor a notice in writing giving such information as was then in the defendant’s possession identifying, or assisting in the identification of, the other person, and the notice is served on the prosecutor at least seven clear days before the hearing of the proceedings or, in Scotland, at least seven clear days before the trial diet. In subsection (3), “advertisement”— means anything published (in any form) for the purpose of promoting a product to the public or a section of the public, and includes a catalogue, a circular and a price list.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.238

text: Subsections (2) and (3) apply where a trader— commits an offence under subsection (1), (2), (3), (6) or (7) of section 237, or would have committed an offence under that subsection but for a defence under section 238, and the commission of the offence, or of what would have been the offence, is due to the act or omission of another person “P”. P commits the offence (whether or not P is a trader and whether or not P’s act or omission is a commercial practice). P may be charged with and convicted of the offence by virtue of subsection (2) whether or not proceedings are taken against the trader. In other provisions of this Chapter (including the rest of this section), references to an offence under subsection (1), (2), (3), (6) or (7) of section 237 include references to an offence under that subsection by virtue of subsection (2). If an offence under section 237 committed by a body corporate is proved— to have been committed with the consent or connivance of an officer of the body, or to be attributable to any neglect on the part of an officer, the officer as well as the body corporate is guilty of the offence and liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly. If the affairs of a body corporate are managed by its members, subsection (5) applies in relation to the acts and defaults of a member in connection with the member’s functions of management as if the member were an officer of the body corporate. If an offence under section 237 committed by a Scottish partnership is proved— to have been committed with the consent or connivance of a partner, or to be attributable to any neglect on the part of a partner, the partner as well as the partnership is guilty of the offence and liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly. In other provisions of this Chapter, references to an offence under section 237 include references to an offence under that section by virtue of subsection (5) or (7). In subsection (5) a reference to an officer of a body corporate includes a reference to— a director, manager, secretary or other similar officer, or a person purporting to act as a director, manager, secretary or other similar officer. In subsection (7), a reference to a partner includes a person purporting to act as a partner.

text: The Secretary of State may by regulations amend Schedule 20 (commercial practices which are in all circumstances considered unfair) so as to— add a description of a commercial practice; remove a description of a commercial practice; amend a description of a commercial practice. text: This section provides for how references to the average consumer are to be read for the purposes of this Chapter. The average consumer is— reasonably well informed, reasonably observant, and reasonably circumspect. The average consumer is to be treated as not knowing information in relation to a commercial practice where such information has been concealed by the trader (even if the average consumer might know the information from another source). Where a commercial practice is directed at a particular group, the average consumer is an average member of that group (and the attributes of the average consumer in subsection (2) are to be read accordingly). This section is subject to section 247.

text: Subsection (2) applies where a group of consumers is particularly vulnerable to a commercial practice in a way that the trader could reasonably be expected to foresee. References in this Chapter to the average consumer, so far as relating to cases to which this subsection applies, are to be read as references to an average member of the group mentioned in subsection (1) (and the attributes of the average consumer in section 246(2) are to be read accordingly). For the purposes of subsection (1), the reference to a group of consumers being particularly vulnerable to a commercial practice— is a reference to the members of the group being particularly vulnerable to the commercial practice causing them to take a transactional decision that they would not have taken otherwise, and includes a reference to a group of consumers being vulnerable to a practice because of the product to which it relates. For the purposes of subsection (1), a group of consumers may be vulnerable as a result of (among other things)— their age; their physical or mental health; their credulity; the circumstances they are in.

text: This Chapter— imposes duties on traders in relation to subscription contracts, provides rights for consumers if those duties are breached, and provides rights for consumers to cancel subscription contracts during cooling-off periods. Sections 254 and 255 set out what is a “subscription contract” for the purposes of this Chapter. Sections 256 to 261 impose duties on traders in relation to subscription contracts. Sections 262 and 263 provide rights for consumers to cancel subscription contracts if traders breach those duties. Sections 264 to 266 provide rights for consumers to cancel subscription contracts during cooling-off periods. Section 267 confers powers to make further provision about the cancellation of subscription contracts under this Chapter. Sections 268 to 271 make provision for the offence of failing to provide information about cooling-off rights. Sections 272 to 281 contain miscellaneous provisions in relation to this Chapter.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.253

text: For the purposes of this Chapter, a subscription contract is a contract between a trader and a consumer— for the supply of goods, services or digital content by the trader to the consumer in exchange for payment by the consumer, to which either or both of subsections (2) and (3) apply, and which is not an excluded contract (see section 255). This subsection applies to a contract if it contains terms which have the effect of providing— for an automatically recurring, or continuing, supply of goods, services or digital content to the consumer for an indefinite period or a fixed period, for the consumer to automatically incur liability for each supply, or recurring liabilities for the continuing supply, and a right for the consumer to bring the contract to an end. This subsection applies to a contract if it contains terms which have the effect of providing— for a supply of goods, services or digital content to a consumer free of charge, or at a rate specified in the contract (the “original rate”), for a period specified in the contract, for the consumer to become automatically liable for payments, or payments at a rate higher than the original rate, for supplies after that period (including where the trader has an option to impose a charge or a higher charge after the end of the period), and a right for the consumer to bring the contract to an end before such liability is incurred. In this Chapter, references to a consumer’s right to bring a subscription contract to an end are references to a right provided under the contract which— in the case of a contract for a fixed period, may be exercised to bring the contract to an end before the end of the fixed period; in any case, may be exercised without the consumer incurring any penalty which is more than nominal, and include references to a right that is expressed in terms of a right to stop a subscription contract from automatically renewing or continuing or any other similar expression.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.254

text: A contract is an excluded contract for the purposes of this Chapter if, and to the extent that, it is of a description set out in Schedule 22. The Secretary of State may by regulations amend Schedule 22 so as to add, remove or modify a description of a contract. The power under subsection (2) includes power to provide for a contract to be an excluded contract— generally for the purposes of this Chapter, or only for such purposes of this Chapter as are specified. Regulations under subsection (2) are subject to the affirmative procedure. See section 275(4) to (8) for how this Chapter applies in relation to a contract that— was an excluded contract at the time it was entered into, and on subsequently ceasing to be an excluded contract, becomes a subscription contract.

text: Before a trader enters into a subscription contract with a consumer, the trader must— give to the consumer the information set out in Part 1 of Schedule 23 (“key pre-contract information”), and give, or make available, to the consumer the information set out in Part 2 of Schedule 23 (“full pre-contract information”). The duty imposed by subsection (1) must be carried out— as close in time to entering into the contract as is practicable, in accordance with subsections (3) and (4), and in accordance with any other requirements specified in regulations under section 277(1)(a). Key pre-contract information must be given under subsection (1)(a) in accordance with the following requirements— it must all be given together; it must be given separately from the full pre-contract information and any other information; in relation to a contract entered into in person, it must be given in writing and on a durable medium; in relation to a contract entered into online and remotely (but not orally), it must be given in writing and in such a way that the consumer is not required to take any steps to read the information, other than the steps the consumer must take to enter into the contract; in relation to a contract entered into orally and remotely, it must be given orally. Full pre-contract information must be given, or made available, under subsection (1)(b) in accordance with the following requirements— it must all be given, or made available, together; in relation to a contract entered into in person, it must be given in writing and on a durable medium. The duty under subsection (1)(b) to give, or make available, full pre-contract information applies in relation to the information set out in paragraphs 14 to 28 of Schedule 23 only to the extent that the information is applicable to the contract and not already apparent from the context. For the purposes of this section, information is made available to a consumer only if the consumer can reasonably be expected to— know how to access it, and be able to access it; For the purposes of this Chapter— references to a contract being entered into in person are references to it being entered into in the simultaneous physical presence of the trader and the consumer; references to a contract being entered into remotely are references to it being entered into without the simultaneous physical presence of the trader and the consumer. The Secretary of State may by regulations amend Parts 1 and 2 of Schedule 23 so as to add, modify or remove descriptions of information. Regulations under subsection (8) are subject to the affirmative procedure.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.256

commentary: S. 256 in force at Royal Assent for specified purposes, see s. 339(2)(c)

text: Subsections (2) and (3) apply in relation to a subscription contract entered into online. The trader must ensure that the final step which the consumer is required to take to enter into the contract involves the consumer expressly acknowledging that the contract imposes an obligation on the consumer to make payments to the trader. The trader must ensure that the information mentioned in subsection (4) is given to a consumer— in writing and in such a way that the consumer is not required to take any steps to read the information, other than the steps the consumer must take to enter into the contract, and in accordance with any other requirement specified in regulations under section 277(1)(a). The information referred to in subsection (3) is— whether there are any restrictions on the delivery of the product to be supplied under the contract, and which means of payment are accepted in relation to the product. If the trader does not comply with subsection (2), the consumer is not bound by the subscription contract. Subsection (7) applies in relation to a subscription contract entered into orally and remotely. If a trader contacts the consumer, the trader must, from the outset, disclose— the trader’s identity, where applicable, the identity of the person on whose behalf the trader is making contact, and the commercial purpose of making contact with the consumer. In cases where— the contract has been entered into in person, and the consumer has signed the contract, the trader must give to the consumer a copy of the signed contract immediately after the consumer has signed the contract. In cases where full pre-contract information has not been given under section 256(1)(b) in writing on a durable medium before the contract is entered into, the trader must give the consumer that information in writing on a durable medium as soon as reasonably practicable after the contract has been entered into and— where goods are to be supplied under the contract, before the supply of any goods; where services are to be supplied under the contract, before the supply of any service.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.257

metadata.act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
commentary: S. 257 not in force at Royal Assent, see s. 339(1)

text: Where a trader enters into a subscription contract with a consumer that does not include a concessionary period, the trader must give to the consumer a notice (referred to in this Chapter as a “reminder notice”) in respect of each renewal payment that relates to the end of a relevant six-month period. A “relevant six-month period” for the purposes of subsection (1) is— the period of 6 months beginning with the day after the day on which the contract was entered into, and each subsequent period of 6 months beginning with the day after the day on which the consumer last became liable for a renewal payment in respect of which a reminder notice was required under subsection (1). Where a trader enters into a subscription contract with a consumer that includes a concessionary period, the trader must give to the consumer a reminder notice in respect of— the first renewal payment for which the consumer will become liable under the contract, and each subsequent renewal payment that relates to the end of a relevant six-month period. A “relevant six-month period” for the purposes of subsection (3) is each period of 6 months beginning with the day after the day on which the consumer last became liable for a renewal payment in respect of which a reminder notice was required under subsection (3). A renewal payment “relates” to the end of a relevant six-month period for the purposes of subsections (1) and (3) if— it is the last (or only) renewal payment for which the consumer becomes liable during that period, or in a case where the consumer does not become liable for any renewal payment during that period, it is the first renewal payment for which the consumer becomes liable after the end of that period. For the purposes of this section a subscription contract includes a concessionary period if it is a contract to which section 254(3) applies. In this Chapter, a “renewal payment”, in relation to a subscription contract, means a payment for which the consumer could avoid liability by exercising a right to bring the contract to an end. Section 259 contains further provision about— the contents of reminder notices, the times at which they must be given, and how they must be given. The Secretary of State may by regulations provide for the requirements imposed by this section and section 259— not to apply in relation to specified descriptions of traders or contracts; to apply subject to modifications in relation to specified descriptions of traders or contracts. Regulations under subsection (9) are subject to the affirmative procedure.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.258

metadata.act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024
commentary: S. 258 in force at Royal Assent for specified purposes, see s. 339(2)(c)

text: A reminder notice must contain— the information set out in Part 3 of Schedule 23, and any other information required by regulations under section 277(1)(b), and that information must be given to the consumer all together. A reminder notice must be given— in accordance with subsections (3) to (8), in such a way that the information referred to in subsection (1) is more prominent than any other information given to the consumer at the same time, and in accordance with any other requirements specified in regulations under section 277(1)(a). A reminder notice must be given within the period specified by the trader for the purposes of this section in the key pre-contract information given to the consumer in relation to the contract (see paragraph 10 of Schedule 23). A period specified in key pre-contract information for the purposes of this section must be a period in advance of the last cancellation date which is reasonable for the purposes of— informing the consumer that they will soon become liable for the renewal payment to which the notice relates, and enabling the consumer to decide whether to bring the subscription contract to an end before incurring that liability (and to take the necessary steps to do so). The “last cancellation date”, in relation to a reminder notice, means the last day on which the consumer could avoid becoming liable for the renewal payment to which the notice relates by exercising a right to bring the contract to an end. Where subsection (7) applies, in addition to giving a reminder notice in accordance with subsection (3), an additional reminder notice must be given— prior to the notice given in accordance with subsection (3), and at a time which is reasonable for the purpose of providing additional notification to the consumer that they will soon become liable for the renewal payment to which the notice relates. This subsection applies where— the consumer will not become liable for a further renewal payment until after the end of the 12-month period, or the consumer will not become liable for any further renewal payment but the contract continues beyond the end of the 12-month period. In subsection (7), the “12-month period” means the period of 12 months beginning with the day before the day on which the consumer will become liable for the renewal payment to which the reminder notice relates.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.259

text: A trader must make arrangements to enable a consumer to exercise a right to bring a subscription contract to an end— in a way which is straightforward, and without having to take any steps which are not reasonably necessary for bringing the contract to an end. A consumer may, alternatively, exercise a right to bring a subscription contract to an end by notifying the trader in accordance with subsection (6) that the consumer is bringing the contract to an end. A consumer may exercise a right to bring a subscription contract to an end at any time permitted by regulations under section 277(1)(c). In relation to a subscription contract entered into online, arrangements under subsection (1) must— enable a consumer to bring the contract to an end online, and ensure that instructions for doing so are displayed online in a place or places that a consumer seeking to end the contract is likely to find them. Arrangements under this section must comply with any other requirements specified in regulations under section 277(1)(c). A notification under subsection (2) may be given by the consumer making a clear statement setting out their decision to bring the contract to an end.

text: This section applies where a consumer— has exercised a right under this Chapter to cancel a subscription contract, or has exercised a right to bring a subscription contract to an end. The trader must— give the consumer a notice acknowledging that fact (referred to in this Chapter as an “end of contract notice”), and if an overpayment has been received by the trader from the consumer, refund that overpayment. An end of contract notice must set out— the date on which the contract was or will be cancelled or on which it came, or will come, to an end, and any other information required by regulations under section 277(1)(b). An end of contract notice must be given— in accordance with subsection (5), in writing on a durable medium, and in accordance with any other requirements specified in regulations under section 277(1)(a). An end of contract notice must be given— before the end of such period as may be specified in regulations under section 277(1)(a), or if no such period is specified— in the case of a consumer exercising a right mentioned in subsection (1) by giving a notification online, before the end of the period of 24 hours from the time that the consumer gives the notification; in a case where the consumer exercises such a right by giving a notification in any other way, before the end of the period of 3 working days beginning with the day after the day that the consumer gives that notification. In subsection (2)(b) “overpayment”, in relation to a subscription contract, means any payment made by the consumer for which the consumer is not liable as a result of cancelling the subscription contract or bringing it to an end.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.261

text: A trader’s compliance with the following duties is an implied term in every subscription contract— the duty set out in section 256(1)(a) (key pre-contract information); the duty set out in section 256(1)(b) (full pre-contract information); the duty set out in section 258 (reminder notices); the duty set out in section 259(4) to specify in key pre-contract information a reasonable period for the giving of a reminder notice under section 259(3) (timing for the giving of reminder notices); the duty set out in section 260(1) (arrangements for consumer to end contract); the duties set out in section 261(2) (end or cancellation of subscription contract).
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.262

text: This section applies where a trader is in breach of the term implied into a subscription contract by section 262(a), (c), (d) or (e). The consumer has the right to cancel the contract. The right is exercisable by the consumer notifying the trader in accordance with subsection (4) that the consumer is cancelling the contract. A notification under subsection (3) may be given by the consumer making a clear statement setting out their decision to cancel the contract. A subscription contract is cancelled from the time the notification is given. Where a subscription contract is cancelled under this section— the cancellation ends both the trader’s and the consumer’s obligations to perform the contract in respect of any rights or liabilities that would arise (but for the cancellation) after the time at which the contract was cancelled, the consumer’s liability for payments that have arisen under the contract is extinguished to any extent set out in regulations under section 267(1)(b) (and, accordingly, the consumer may be entitled to a refund), and any other provision made under those regulations in relation to the treatment of goods, services or digital content supplied under a cancelled subscription contract applies. No penalty or charge may be imposed on a consumer for cancelling a subscription contract under subsection (2). For further provision about the exercise of a right to cancel under this section, see section 267.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.263

text: A consumer has the right to cancel a subscription contract during— the initial cooling-off period, and any renewal cooling-off period. The right conferred by subsection (1)— is exercisable in any circumstances, and may not be subject to any conditions other than those set out in or under this Chapter. The right is exercisable by the consumer notifying the trader in accordance with subsection (4) that the consumer is cancelling the contract. A notification under subsection (3) may be given by the consumer making a clear statement setting out their decision to cancel the contract. A subscription contract is cancelled from the time that such a notification is given. Where a subscription contract is cancelled under this section— the cancellation ends both the consumer’s and the trader’s obligations to perform the contract in respect of any rights or liabilities that would arise (but for the cancellation) after the time at which the contract was cancelled, the consumer’s liability for payments that have arisen under the contract is extinguished to any extent set out in regulations under section 267(1)(b) (and, accordingly, the consumer may be entitled to a refund), and any other provision made under those regulations in relation to the treatment of goods, services or digital content supplied under a cancelled subscription contract applies. No penalty or charge may be imposed on a consumer for cancelling a subscription contract under subsection (1). For further provision about the exercise of a right to cancel under this section, see section 267.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.264

text: In this Chapter, the “initial cooling-off period”, in relation to a subscription contract, means the period— beginning with the day the contract is entered into, and ending— in the case of a contract under which goods are supplied, at the end of the period of 14 days beginning with the day after the day on which the consumer receives the first supply of goods under the contract; in any other case, at the end of the period of 14 days beginning with the day after the day on which the contract is entered into. In this Chapter, a “renewal cooling-off period”, in relation to a subscription contract, means a period— beginning with the day on which a relevant renewal of the contract occurs, and ending at the end of the period of 14 days beginning with the day after that day. A “relevant renewal” of a subscription contract occurs for the purposes of subsection (2)— when the consumer becomes liable under the contract for a first renewal payment following the end of a concessionary period, or at any time when the consumer becomes liable under the contract for a renewal payment and either— the consumer will not become liable for the next renewal payment until after the end of the 12-month period, or the consumer will not become liable for any further renewal payment but the contract continues beyond the end of the 12-month period. In subsection (3)— in paragraph (a), “concessionary period” means a period of time mentioned in section 254(3)(a), and in paragraph (b), the “12-month period” means the period of 12 months beginning with the day before the day on which the consumer became liable for the renewal payment. For the purposes of subsection (1)(b)(i), the first supply of goods under a subscription contract is not to be treated as having taken place until such time as the consumer receives all of the goods that the consumer is due to receive as part of that supply. This section is subject to such extensions of a cooling-off period as may be provided for by regulations under section 267(1)(c).
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.265

text: In relation to each renewal cooling-off period, a trader must give the consumer a notice (referred to in this Chapter as a “cooling-off notice”). A cooling-off notice must set out— that the subscription contract is continuing, that the consumer has a right to cancel the subscription contract during the cooling-off period to which the notice relates, when that period begins and ends, how the consumer may exercise the right to cancel, if the consumer may lose the right, the circumstances under which that will happen, the consequences of the consumer exercising the right, including— any refund the consumer may be entitled to, any reason that refund might be diminished, and in respect of a contract for the supply of goods, whether the consumer will be responsible for returning those goods to the trader, and any other information required by regulations under section 277(1)(b). A cooling-off notice must be given— on the first day of the renewal cooling-off period to which it relates or as soon as reasonably practicable after that day, separately from the giving of any other information, and in accordance with any other requirements specified in regulations under section 277(1)(a).
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.266

metadata.act_title: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024

text: The Secretary of State may by regulations make provision— about the exercise of the rights of a consumer to cancel a subscription contract under this Chapter; about the consequences that follow a consumer exercising such rights; extending a cooling-off period in such cases, and to such extent, as the regulations may specify. Regulations under subsection (1)(a) may include provision— requiring a right to cancel to be exercised before the end of a specified period; imposing other conditions or restrictions on the exercise of a right to cancel (for example, provision that a consumer may lose the right to cancel a subscription contract during a cooling-off period if they choose to be supplied with digital content or services under the contract during that period). Regulations under subsection (1)(b) may include provision— setting out the extent to which a consumer’s liability for payments that have arisen under a cancelled subscription contract is extinguished; as a consequence of provision made under paragraph (a), requiring a trader to refund a consumer for payments the consumer has made under the contract; treating the consumer as having paid for goods, services or digital content received under a cancelled subscription contract; about the trader’s right to recover goods or digital content that have been supplied under a cancelled subscription contract; setting out the consequences of a consumer— bringing a subscription contract to an end at a time when the consumer has one or more rights to cancel the contract under this Chapter; cancelling a subscription contract at a time when the consumer has more than one right to cancel the contract under this Chapter. Provision under subsection (3)(a) and (b) may secure the result (for example, in cases where a consumer has been supplied with digital content or services under a contract before it is cancelled during a cooling-off period) that— the consumer remains liable (partly or fully) for payments falling due before the cancellation of the contract, and the consumer is entitled to a reduced or no refund. Provision under subsection (3)(e)(ii) must secure the result that, unless the consumer chooses otherwise, the consumer is to be taken to exercise the right to cancel under this Chapter that results in the most advantageous remedy to the consumer (and the regulations may include provision for determining what remedy is “most advantageous” to a consumer in different descriptions of case). Before making regulations under subsection (1)(c), the Secretary of State must consult such persons as the Secretary of State considers appropriate. The following regulations under this section are subject to the affirmative procedure— the first regulations to be made under this section; any other regulations under this section that include provision within subsection (1)(c). Regulations under this section to which subsection (7) does not apply are subject to the negative procedure.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.267

text: A trader commits an offence if the trader— enters into an off-premises subscription contract, and fails to— give the consumer the information listed in paragraph 11(a) of Schedule 23 in accordance with section 256(1)(a), or give, or make available, the information set out in paragraph 21 of that Schedule in accordance with section 256(1)(b). Subsections (3) and (4) apply where a trader— commits an offence under subsection (1), or would have committed an offence under that subsection but for a defence under section 269, and the commission of the offence, or of what would have been the offence, is due to the act or omission of another person (“P”). P commits the offence (whether or not P is a trader). P may be charged with and convicted of the offence by virtue of subsection (3) whether or not proceedings are taken against the trader. In this section, an “off-premises subscription contract” means a subscription contract— entered into in person, in a place which is not the business premises of the trader, entered into by any means immediately after the consumer was individually and personally addressed by the trader in person in a place which is not the business premises of the trader, or entered into during an excursion organised by the trader with the aim or effect of promoting and selling goods or services to the consumer. In subsection (5), “business premises”, in relation to a trader, means— any immovable retail premises where the activity of the trader is carried out on a permanent basis, or any movable retail premises where the activity of the trader is carried out on a usual basis. In other provisions of this Chapter, references to an offence under subsection (1) include references to an offence under that subsection by virtue of subsection (3).

text: It is a defence for a person (“the defendant”) charged with an offence under section 268(1) to prove— that the commission of the offence was due to— the act or omission of another person, or reliance on information given by another person, and that the defendant took all reasonable precautions and exercised all due diligence to avoid the commission of such an offence by the defendant or any other person under the defendant’s control. A defendant is not entitled to rely on the defence provided by subsection (1) without the permission of the court unless— the defendant has served on the prosecutor a notice in writing giving such information as was then in the defendant’s possession identifying, or assisting in the identification of, the other person, and the notice is served on the prosecutor at least seven clear days before the hearing of the proceedings or, in Scotland, at least seven clear days before the trial diet.

text: If an offence under section 268(1) committed by a body corporate is proved— to have been committed with the consent or connivance of an officer of the body, or to be attributable to any neglect on the officer’s part, the officer as well as the body corporate is guilty of the offence and liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly. In subsection (1) a reference to an officer of a body corporate includes a reference to— a director, manager, secretary or other similar officer; a person purporting to act as a director, manager, secretary or other similar officer. If the affairs of a body corporate are managed by its members, subsection (1) applies in relation to the acts and defaults of a member in connection with the member’s functions of management as if the member were an officer of the body corporate. Where an offence under section 268(1) committed by a Scottish partnership is proved— to have been committed with the consent or connivance of a partner, or to be attributable to any neglect on the part of a partner, the partner as well as the partnership is guilty of the offence and liable to be proceeded against and punished accordingly. In subsection (4), a reference to a partner includes a person purporting to act as a partner.

text: A person who is guilty of an offence under section 268(1) is liable— on summary conviction in England Wales, to a fine; on summary conviction in Scotland or Northern Ireland, to a fine not exceeding level 5 on the standard scale. It is the duty of every local weights and measures authority in Great Britain to enforce section 268(1) in its area. It is the duty of the Department for the Economy in Northern Ireland to enforce section 268(1) in Northern Ireland. No proceedings for an offence under section 268(1) may be instituted in England and Wales except by or on behalf of a local weights and measures authority in Great Britain. Nothing in subsection (2) authorises any local weights and measures authority in Great Britain to bring proceedings in Scotland for an offence.

text: This section applies for the purposes of this Chapter. Where a trader gives any information or notice under this Chapter by email, by a message sent online, or by any other means of electronic communication, the information or notice is to be treated as given by the trader, and as received by the consumer, at the time that the communication is sent to the consumer. Subsection (2) applies even if the consumer does not receive the communication where the reason for that is beyond the control of the trader. Subsection (5) applies for the purposes of determining whether a consumer has— given notice that the consumer is cancelling a subscription contract in exercise of a right conferred by this Chapter within the period of time specified for the consumer to exercise the right; given notice that the consumer is bringing a subscription contract to an end within a period of time, or before a date, specified or described in the contract as the period during which, or date before which, the consumer may exercise the right. The consumer is to be treated as having given notice within the required period, or before the specified date, if the communication by which the notice is given is sent before the end of that period or date (and for this purpose it is immaterial whether or not the trader receives the notice). The burden of proof lies with the trader in any dispute between the trader and a consumer as to whether information or a notice has been given by the trader to the consumer in accordance with this Chapter. The burden of proof lies with the consumer in any dispute between the consumer and a trader as to— whether the consumer has notified the trader that the consumer is bringing to an end, or cancelling, a subscription contract in accordance with this Chapter; when the consumer gave such notice. Any information that a trader gives to a consumer under this Chapter must be given in clear and plain language and if given in writing, be in a legible form; if given orally, be audible and comprehensible.
citation: Digital Markets, Competition and Consumers Act 2024 (2024 c.13) s.272
